newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Greycoat wants to get on with work.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Greycoat wants to get on with work.

text.p: Embattled UK property company Greycoat Plc said on Thursday it hoped to get on with its normal business rather than deal with the demands of rebel shareholders, who had wanted to break up the group.

"It has cost us a lot of money and a lot of wasted effort and time. What we would like to do is get on with running a property company," Peter Thornton, Greycoat's chief executive told Reuters of the attempt by the UK Active Value Fund (UKAV).
Thornton was speaking after a vote by Greycoat shareholders on UKAV's resolution calling for the sale of all Greycoat's assets. He said he was confident they would reject the plan.

On Wednesday, UKAV said it would abstain from voting at the reconvened extraordinary general meeting called to vote on its resolution. Greycoat's chairman Michael Beckett told the meeting the cost of the exercise had been around 300,000 stg.
This, he said, amounted to the equivalent of around a 20 percent increase in the firm's dividend.

Beckett told the meeting that more than 35 million proxy votes had been cast against the break-up resolution, while just over four million had voted in favour of it. The final result is expected by 1400 GMT.

Thornton welcomed the fact that one phase of the uncertainty currently surrounding the group was over. He said Greycoat had yet to receive the answers needed from smaller rival Moorfield Estates, which has put forward a merger proposal.

"We still haven't received answers to our 30-odd questions," he said of the Moorfield approach, adding Greycoat was not prepared to embark on a due diligence exercise or open its books to Moorfield without more concrete details of the firm's plans.
"They have yet to convince us they have got some proposals that actually work," Thornton said. Moorfield has suggested demerging Greycoat's largest assets.

The current focus on Greycoat is centred on its two largest properties, Embankment Place on the River Thames, near London's Charing Cross station and 123 Buckingham Palace Road, to the west of the city.
Since the proposal by UKAV to break-up the group's 500 million stg portfolio surfaced in October, Greycoat has said it was already looking at selling Embankment Place.
"We'd always planned, at the right time, to sell Embankment Place. So it is nothing new to us," Thornton said, adding that he could not say how close the sale of the property now was.
"No-one knows how close it is," he said.
Thornton said relations with potential purchasers had been established but there were fairly few buyers in the world able to pay more than 200 million stg.

He said that now the sale was out in the open it would affect the perception of buyers as it was no longer an off-market transaction. He said he could not quantify how much this might shave off the sale price.

But with a valuation of 217 million stg, outstanding debt of 141 million stg and debt swap costs of 10 million stg if the property is sold, Thornton said an assertion by UKAV that 100 million stg could be returned to shareholders was wrong.

The real amount that shareholders would receive would be more like 60 million stg, and this could be returned through a buy-back or some other format. But he dismissed the possibility of a dividend payout.
While Greycoat's 123 Buckingham Palace Road property was not currently on the "For Sale" list, Thornton said that anything in the portfolio was always for sale if the price was right.
The property had last been valued at 84.25 million stg.
-- Alexander Smith, London Newsroom ++ 44 171 542 7719
